extracted.intended_audience: policy makers, federal agency staff, legal and regulatory researchers, and members of the public interested in federal information-quality rules
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding and implementing the statutory and procedural requirements of the Data Quality Act (Information Quality Act) for federal agencies: what standards information disseminated by agencies must meet and what administrative processes agencies must provide for correction, peer review, and reporting. Useful for drafting agency guidelines, compliance checks, or preparing administrative petitions under the IQA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality, Objectivity, Utility, and Integrity of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: "provide policy and procedural guidance to federal agencies for ensuring and maximizing the quality, objectivity, utility, and integrity of information (including statistical information) disseminated by Federal agencies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory standard. It applies to all information disseminated by federal agencies (including statistical information). Agency guidelines and OMB guidance are intended to operationalize what each of these terms means in practice (e.g., standards for data collection, documentation, transparency, and analytic methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB issuance of government-wide guidelines (with public and agency involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Director of the Office of Management and Budget shall, by not later than September 30, 2001, and with public and Federal agency involvement, issue guidelines..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB is responsible for creating government-wide guidance that agencies must follow; the statute contemplates public and agency input in developing those guidelines. The OMB final and draft guideline documents (e.g., Oct 1, 2001; corrected final guidelines in Fed. Reg. Feb. 22, 2002) set baseline expectations across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines must apply to sharing and access to disseminated information
rubrics_metrics.description: "(b)(1) apply to the sharing by Federal agencies of, and access to, information disseminated by Federal agencies;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IQA coverage includes not only initial dissemination but also subsequent sharing and public access to agency information; agencies should ensure consistent quality standards across formats and distribution channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency deadline to issue their own information-quality guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: "(b)(2)(A) issue guidelines ensuring and maximizing the quality, objectivity, utility, and integrity of information (including statistical information) disseminated by the agency, by not later than 1 year after the date of issuance of the guidelines under subsection (a);"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each federal agency is required to adopt its own information-quality guidelines within one year after OMB issues government-wide guidelines. Agency guidelines are expected to adapt OMB standards to the agency's programs, data types, and dissemination practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative mechanisms to seek and obtain correction of information
rubrics_metrics.description: "(b)(2)(B) establish administrative mechanisms allowing affected persons to seek and obtain correction of information maintained and disseminated by the agency that does not comply with the guidelines issued under subsection (a);"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must provide a process (often a petition process) by which individuals or entities affected by agency information can request correction. Guidance should describe how to submit a petition, the grounds for correction, timelines, and remedies. This is the principal administrative remedy contemplated by the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic reporting to OMB about complaints and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: "(b)(2)(C) report periodically to the Director -- (i) the number and nature of complaints received by the agency regarding the accuracy of information disseminated by the agency; and (ii) how such complaints were handled by the agency."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must track and report metrics about petitions/complaints (counts, subject matter, and disposition). These reports allow OMB oversight of implementation; agency guidance should specify recordkeeping and reporting formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to publish peer-review agendas and related guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Other federal agencies are also required to publish their own guidelines for information quality and peer review agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IQA/OMB framework envisions coordination between information-quality guidance and formal peer review processes. Agencies should publish peer-review plans/agendas and integrate peer review where appropriate to support objectivity and integrity of influential scientific information.

rubrics_metrics.name: No private right of action / limits on judicial review under the IQA
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have held that the IQA does not provide a private cause of action and that challenges to information quality should proceed through administrative mechanisms rather than in courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases cited (e.g., dismissal of Competitive Enterprise Institute v. EPA; In re Operation of the Missouri River System litigation; Salt Institute suits) and DOJ briefs reiterate that IQA does not create statutory judicial review rights. Practitioners should expect administrative remedies, not litigation under IQA alone, and consider APA or other bases if seeking court review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of misuse: vehicle for special-interest challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Data Quality Act has been criticized as providing a vehicle for special interest groups to challenge regulations on the grounds of not meeting information quality requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue the IQA can be used tactically to delay or disrupt rulemaking by attacking underlying information. The article notes commentary (e.g., Jim Tozzi acknowledging industry funding) and examples of attempts to use IQA petitions to affect agency outputs. Agencies should design petition and correction procedures to focus on substantive quality defects and to avoid procedural gamesmanship; petitioners should be clear about substantive errors versus policy disagreement.
